# Section 3: missingness information and multiple imputation

Now that the clean dataset has been created, I am going to generate missingness tables and impute datasets for analyses.

Note that if you are not directly working with data from above (for instance, if you have to load the output from the previous step into R), you can read in the .csv file, but if you have been working with the data from above you can simply continue below.

```{r}
#| label: final-load
#| code-summary: Reading in the cleaned file
# reading in .csv file if needed
# UKHLS_analytic <- read.csv("UKHLS_analytic_20260812.csv")
```

## Obtaining missingness information (pre-imputation)

First, we'll create a missingness summary table before imputation with all the values in the table.

```{r}
#| label: missingness-summary
#| code-summary: Generating and exporting missingness table
missingness_summary <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), 
                   ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "Variable", 
               values_to = "Missing_n") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_n = nrow(UKHLS_analytic),
    Missing_percent = round((Missing_n / Total_n) * 100, 2),
    Complete_n = Total_n - Missing_n,
    Complete_percent = round((Complete_n / Total_n) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing_percent)) %>%
  select(Variable, Total_n, Complete_n, Complete_percent, Missing_n, Missing_percent)
print(missingness_summary, n = Inf)
```

Before imputation, we also figured it would be worth having a rough estimate of how many cells were missing, too, to see the levels of imputation potentially needed.

```{r}
#| label: total-missing-cells
#| code-summary: Quick tabulation of total missing cells
# total missing cells across entire dataset
sum(is.na(UKHLS_analytic))
# total cells in dataset
nrow(UKHLS_analytic) * ncol(UKHLS_analytic)
# percentage missing
percent_missing <- (sum(is.na(UKHLS_analytic)) / 
                      (nrow(UKHLS_analytic) * ncol(UKHLS_analytic))) * 100
percent_missing
```

Finally, we also wanted to obtain missing and complete proportions for each exposure and outcome variable.

```{r}
#| label: exposure-check-build
#| code-summary: Missingness per exposure variable calculation
exposure_vars_check <- c("family_3plus", "treated", "post_policy_month",
                         "time_since_policy", "intyear", "age_youngest_child",
                         "n_children_u18", "n_children_5_under",
                         "youngest_child_yob", "any_third_plus_2017")

exposure_check <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(exposure_vars_check), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_n") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_n = nrow(UKHLS_analytic),
    Missing_percent = round((Missing_n / Total_n) * 100, 2),
    Complete_n = Total_n - Missing_n,
    Complete_percent = round((Complete_n / Total_n) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  select(Variable, Total_n, Complete_n, Complete_percent, Missing_n, Missing_percent)
# print as a table
print(exposure_check, n = Inf)
```

We then figured it made sense to obtain a similar proportion to above, but counting missingness and completeness for each outcome.

```{r}
#| label: outcome-check-build
#| code-summary: Missingness per outcome calculation
outcome_vars_check <- c("GHQ_total", "SF_total", "self_health", "health_sat",
                        "life_sat", "finnow", "finfut")

outcome_check <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(outcome_vars_check), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_n") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_n = nrow(UKHLS_analytic),
    Missing_percent = round((Missing_n / Total_n) * 100, 2),
    Complete_n = Total_n - Missing_n,
    Complete_percent = round((Complete_n / Total_n) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  select(Variable, Total_n, Complete_n, Complete_percent, Missing_n, Missing_percent)
# checking as table
print(outcome_check, n = Inf)
```

I then export missingness tables with all the information above.

```{r}
#| label: missingness-export
#| code-summary: Exporting missingness tables
wb_missing <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb_missing, "Summary")
writeData(wb_missing, "Summary", missingness_summary)
addWorksheet(wb_missing, "Exposure")
writeData(wb_missing, "Exposure", exposure_check)
addWorksheet(wb_missing, "Outcomes")
writeData(wb_missing, "Outcomes", outcome_check)
saveWorkbook(wb_missing, "output/Missingness_pre_20260812.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

We have decided that, to ensure an equal N across all outcomes, we are imputing missing values for the outcomes where there are values missing. Now, we are going onto the imputation step.

## Imputation setup and implementation

### Preparing data for imputation

```{r}
#| label: imp-col-names
#| code-summary: Calling column names function
colnames(UKHLS_analytic)
id_vars         <- c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename")
exposure_vars   <- c("age_youngest_child", "n_children_5_under", "family_3plus", "treated",
                     "post_policy_month", "intyear",
                     "time_since_policy", "any_third_plus_2017")
design_vars     <- c("psu", "strata", "xs_weight")
outcome_vars    <- c("GHQ_total", "SF_total", "self_health", "health_sat",
                     "life_sat", "finnow", "finfut")
confounder_vars <- c("age", "sex", "ethn_binary", "ukborn", "urban",
                     "edu_qual", "marstat", "equiv_yearly", "oc_current", "chron_health")
```

```{r}
#| label: imp-build-df
#| code-summary: Building dataframe that will go into imputation
df <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  select(all_of(c(id_vars, exposure_vars, design_vars, outcome_vars, confounder_vars))) %>%
  # nominal covariates - converted to factors so MICE imputes them with a categorical model rather than matching on an arbitrary numeric code, and so that any model using them estimates a coefficient per category. "oc_current" is only partly ordered: 1-3 follow the NS-SEC hierarchy but 4-5 (long-/short-term unemployed) are a different state, not further steps down it. "edu_qual" is left numeric: it is ordinal, and with "none" recoded from 9 to 6, the categories are evenly spaced on the attainment ranking
  mutate(across(c(marstat, oc_current), as.factor))

# drop any column that is entirely missing - MICE cannot model these
df <- df %>% select(where(~ !all(is.na(.x))))

# held out of imputation but retained; everything else is imputed
dont_impute <- c(id_vars, exposure_vars, design_vars)

# anything in UKHLS_analytic not entering imputation - check nothing needed is missing
setdiff(names(UKHLS_analytic), names(df))

# held-out variables keep their missingness - these rows drop listwise from any model using them
colSums(is.na(df[, intersect(dont_impute, names(df))]))
```

### Initialising MICE

The kind of imputation I'll be using here is multiple imputation using chained equations (MICE). I first set up the MICE and check if there are any logged events (potential problems with data and what corrective action MICE took).

```{r}
#| label: imp-init
#| code-summary: Initialising MICE
ini <- mice(df, maxit = 0, print = FALSE)
meth <- ini$method
pred <- ini$predictorMatrix
```

```{r}
#| label: imp-logged-events
#| code-summary: Checking what the logged events are
ini$loggedEvents
```

### Set imputation method and predictor matrix

Since we are not imputing ID variable(s), exposure-related variables or design-related variables, I am making that distinction clear here.

```{r}
#| label: imp-dont-impute
#| code-summary: Making imputed and non-imputed columns distinct
dont_impute <- intersect(dont_impute, names(meth))  # guard against dropped columns
meth[dont_impute]   <- ""   # do not impute these
pred[, dont_impute] <- 1    # but do use them as predictors for everything else
diag(pred) <- 0             # no variable predicts itself
pred[, c(id_vars, "psu", "strata")] <- 0 # not using ID variables or the design labels as predictors (as they're just labels, not substantive predictors)
# the survey weight is retained as a predictor so that the imputation model is congenial with the weighted sensitivity analyses, which is standard practice for multiple imputation under a complex survey design. it is complete after the weight construction in section 2, so it does not reduce the data available to any imputation model
# dropping redundant date and exposure predictors, which otherwise make the predictor matrix near-singular and trigger mice's ridge penalty on every imputation. "time_since_policy" is retained as the finest-grained of the three date variables, and "intyear" and "post_policy_month" are both deterministic functions of it. "treated" is 0 for every 1-2 child family, so "family_3plus" predicts it perfectly on that half
pred[, c("intyear", "post_policy_month", "treated")] <- 0
```

I decided to use single-level imputation for all variables to be imputed, as household clustering is still accounted for in analysis (`feols` models use `cluster = ~hidp`). This mostly uses predictive-mean matching (PMM) for continuous and ordinal outcomes, and polyreg for those without ordering.

```{r}
#| label: imp-method-pmm
#| code-summary: Setting imputation method by variable type
# method by variable type, all single-level:
# - nominal covariates (marstat, oc_current): multinomial logistic regression
# - continuous and ordinal (including edu_qual and all outcomes): predictive mean matching
impute_vars  <- names(meth)[meth != ""]   # defined once, from what MICE will actually do
nominal_vars <- intersect(c("marstat", "oc_current"), impute_vars)
meth[setdiff(impute_vars, nominal_vars)] <- "pmm"
meth[nominal_vars] <- "polyreg"
meth  # inspect before running

# should be empty - anything returned was dropped by MICE for collinearity
setdiff(names(meth)[meth == ""], dont_impute)
```

I've commented it out in this code, but if you wanted to run a test first, I've set the following parameters for this test run:

- `m=2`: generating two datasets

- `maxit=5`: algorithm runs five iterations

Diagnostics checked via `plot(imp_test)`, `stripplot(imp_test)`, and `densityplot(imp_test)`.

```{r}
#| label: imp-test-run
#| code-summary: Imputation test run
# test run first: m=2, maxit=5
imp_test <- mice(df, m = 2, maxit = 5, method = meth, 
                predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 123, print = TRUE)


# check diagnostic
plot(imp_test)
stripplot(imp_test)

# running another diagnostic at m = 2, maxit = 20 to see nonconvergence
# imp_test_2 <- mice(df, m = 2, maxit = 10, method = meth, 
#                predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 123, print = TRUE)

# check diagnostic
#plot(imp_test_2)
#stripplot(imp_test_2)
```

### Full imputation

If test looks good, run full imputation: `m = 20` (doing this because of interaction terms), `maxit = 15` (because the convergence plots were only just starting to even out slope-wise at `maxit = 10`). This can be quite heavy computationally, so be careful!

```{r}
#| label: imp-full-run
#| code-summary: Running full imputation
imp <- mice(df, m = 20, maxit = 15, method = meth, 
            predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 123, print = TRUE)
# checking logged events, if any
imp$loggedEvents 
```

```{r}
#| label: imp-convergence-plot
#| code-summary: Generating convergence plots for visual inspection
pdf("output/mice_convergence_plots_20260812.pdf", width = 10, height = 8)
plot(imp)
dev.off()
```

Now, following successful imputation and inspection of convergence plots, I save the full imputed object – *instead of running the imputation each time, you should reload this saved object after you've done imputation!*

```{r}
#| label: imp-save-object
#| code-summary: Saving imputation object
# save imputation object (all 20 datasets)
saveRDS(imp, "UKHLS_imputation_object_20260812.rds")
```

### Imputation diagnostics (and troubleshooting if necessary)

After the imputation object has been created, I run some troubleshooting.

First, I verifying the number of NAs for all imputed variables - this should see zero.

```{r}
#| label: imp-verify-no-na
#| code-summary: Verifying NAs
imp_missing <- mice::complete(imp, "long") %>%
  group_by(.imp) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(impute_vars), ~sum(is.na(.))))
print(imp_missing, width = Inf)
```

**For if there are any missing values remaining:** extract the observations with any remaining NAs from dataset 1 (because the missingness pattern will be the same across all datasets).

```{r}
#| label: imp-missing-troubleshoot
#| code-summary: Troubleshooting non-imputed missingness
#missing_obs <- mice::complete(imp, 1) %>%
#  filter(if_any(all_of(impute_vars), is.na))

# view them
#view(missing_obs)
```

### Post-imputation data management

First, stack all datasets (including original) for manipulation purposes, here I am using `include = TRUE` so we get datasets 0–20.

```{r}
#| label: imp-stack-long
#| code-summary: Stacking all datasets for data management
imp_long <- mice::complete(imp, "long", include = TRUE)  # WITH include=TRUE (datasets 0-20)
```

Remember earlier how I'd mentioned we'd need to recalculate income quintiles for all datasets since you have different values now? Now would be the time to do that.

```{r}
#| label: imp-recalc-quintiles
#| code-summary: Re-calculating income quintile distributions given imputed data
imp_long <- imp_long %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%  # group by imputation and year
  mutate(
    income_quintile = if_else(.imp == 0, NA_integer_, ntile(equiv_yearly, 5)),
    income_decile   = if_else(.imp == 0, NA_integer_, ntile(equiv_yearly, 10))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

I want to highlight this following step as it's incredibly important - these outcomes will be the ones used for our analyses, and the plan is to report both raw and standardised outcomes - but I then standardise within each imputed dataset.

```{r}
#| label: imp-zscore-outcomes
#| code-summary: Creating z-score standardisation for outcomes
imp_long_full <- imp_long %>%
  group_by(.imp) %>%  # standardising within each imputed dataset
  mutate(across(all_of(outcome_vars),
                ~if_else(.imp == 0, NA_real_, scale(.x)[,1]),
                .names = "{.col}_z")) %>%
  ungroup()
```

### Saving `imp_long_full` and `imp_complete` datasets

You'll need both versions, because depending on the kind of analysis you're doing (descriptive or inferential statistics), you'll be using one or the other.

For reference:

- `imp_long_full` - contains original and all imputed 20 datasets put together one after the other

- `imp_complete` - contains imputation object with original and imputed datasets

```{r}
#| label: imp-save-long
#| code-summary: Saving datasets
saveRDS(imp_long_full, "UKHLS_imputation_long_20260812.rds")

imp_complete <- as.mids(imp_long_full)
# save imputation objects (all datasets)
saveRDS(imp_complete, "UKHLS_imputation_sets_20260812.rds")
```

# Section 4: descriptives and analysis

Now we can run the full sample analyses on the prepared dataset for policy evaluation. Prior to this, there is a setup block of code that should be run to make sure that any analysis block can afterwards be run on its own.

As a reminder, the labels used correspond to the following outcomes:

**Mental health**

- `GHQ_total` -\> psychological distress

- `life_sat` -\> life satisfaction

**General health**

- `self_health` -\> self-rated health

- `SF_total` -\> health-related quality of life (HRQoL)

- `health_sat` -\> health satisfaction

**Financial health**

- `finnow` -\> financial situation

- `finfut` -\> financial outlook

We conduct the analyses including terms for panel weights:

- `xs_weight` - cross-sectional weight constructed above

- `strata` - sampling stratum

- `svyglm()` instead of `feols()` because the `fixest` package does not support survey designs

(NB Understanding Society does not include population-wide correction terms.)

```{r}
#| label: analysis-setup
#| code-summary: Analysis setup

# load the imputed long dataset (skip if Section 3 was just run)
imp_long_full <- readRDS("UKHLS_imputation_long_20260812.rds")
imp_complete <- readRDS("UKHLS_imputation_sets_20260812.rds")

# number of imputations - derived rather than hardcoded, used in pooling below
m_imp <- max(imp_long_full$.imp)
m_imp # should say 20

# DiD windows - read by the parallel trends test and the power analysis below
did_pre  <- 2014:2016
did_post <- 2023:2025

# filter out 2017 births in 3+ children group for main analysis
imp_long_no2017 <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(!(family_3plus == 1 & any_third_plus_2017 == 1))
imp_no2017 <- as.mids(imp_long_no2017)
# counted on the observed data only, since imp_long_full stacks the 20 imputed datasets on top of it
imp_long_no2017 %>% filter(.imp == 0) %>% record_flow("Excluding 3+ families with a third or more child born in 2017")

# ITS-specific mids object (3+ families only) - works because family_3plus is not imputed
imp_long_its <- imp_long_no2017 %>% filter(family_3plus == 1)
imp_its <- as.mids(imp_long_its)

# parallel trends: the pre-policy years, tested as a difference in annual trend between groups rather than a contrast between two lumped periods
# works because intyear is not imputed, so the same rows drop from every .imp
pt_years <- 2009:2016

imp_long_pt <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(intyear %in% pt_years) %>%
  mutate(pt_year = intyear - max(pt_years))   # centred on the last pre-policy year
imp_pt <- as.mids(imp_long_pt)

# outcome metadata vectors - defined here for use throughout script
outcomes_raw   <- c("GHQ_total", "life_sat", "self_health", "SF_total", "health_sat", "finnow", "finfut")
outcome_labels <- c("Psychological distress", "Life satisfaction", "Self-rated health", "HRQoL", "Health satisfaction", "Financial situation", "Financial outlook")

# appending z-score suffix to outcome variable names (used later for z-score figures)
outcomes_z_names <- paste0(outcomes_raw, "_z")

# format pooled model result as "estimate (lower, upper)" for export tables
format_result <- function(pooled_model, term_name) {
  s <- summary(pooled_model, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>%
    filter(term == term_name)
  if (nrow(s) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  sprintf("%.3f (%.3f, %.3f)",
          s$estimate,
          s$`5 %`,
          s$`95 %`)
}

# extract legend from a ggplot as a standalone panel (used in multi-panel figures)
make_legend_panel <- function(plot_obj) {
  tmp <- plot_obj + 
    guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1), shape = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
          legend.title = element_blank(),
          legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
          legend.spacing.y = unit(0.1, "cm"))
  legend_grob <- cowplot::get_legend(tmp)
  cowplot::ggdraw(legend_grob)
}

# assigning y-axis labels for figures (parentheticals indicate higher = worse direction for reverse-coded outcomes)
outcome_ylabs <- c(
  "(Worse) psychological distress",
  "(Lower) life satisfaction",
  "(Lower) self-rated health",
  "(Worse) HRQoL",
  "(Lower) health satisfaction",
  "(Worse) financial situation",
  "(Worse) financial outlook"
)

# covariate values for marginal means, taken as design-matrix column means rather than means of the raw variables. this handles factors correctly - a dummy's column mean is simply its proportion, and its name matches the model's own coefficient name
covariate_means <- function(data_long, cov_formula, n_imp_use = 5) {
  xb <- lapply(seq_len(n_imp_use), function(i) {
    X <- model.matrix(cov_formula, data = data_long %>% filter(.imp == i))
    colMeans(X)
  })
  rowMeans(do.call(cbind, xb))
}

# contrast vector for one cell: intercept 1, covariates at their means, design terms at the requested values, everything else 0
build_L <- function(coef_names, xbar, design_values) {
  L <- setNames(rep(0, length(coef_names)), coef_names)
  shared <- intersect(names(xbar), coef_names)
  L[shared] <- xbar[shared]
  L["(Intercept)"] <- 1
  for (nm in names(design_values)) {
    if (nm %in% coef_names) L[nm] <- design_values[[nm]]
  }
  L
}

# marginal means from the individual fits: mu = L'beta, se = sqrt(L' V L) using the cluster-robust vcov, pooled across imputations with the same Rubin's rules as above (within = mean(se^2), between = var(est))
marginal_means_fits <- function(model_list, xbar, grid, design_fn) {
  per_imp <- lapply(model_list, function(m) {
    b <- coef(m); V <- vcov(m)
    t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(k) {
      L <- build_L(names(b), xbar, design_fn(grid[k, , drop = FALSE]))
      c(est = as.numeric(L %*% b),
        se  = sqrt(as.numeric(t(L) %*% V %*% L)))
    }, numeric(2)))
  })
  est <- do.call(cbind, lapply(per_imp, function(x) x[, "est"]))
  se  <- do.call(cbind, lapply(per_imp, function(x) x[, "se"]))
  pooled_est <- rowMeans(est)
  pooled_se  <- sqrt(rowMeans(se^2) + (1 + 1/m_imp) * apply(est, 1, var))
  cbind(grid,
        data.frame(pooled_mean = pooled_est,
                   pooled_se   = pooled_se,
                   ci_lower    = pooled_est - 1.645 * pooled_se,
                   ci_upper    = pooled_est + 1.645 * pooled_se))
}

# covariate formula, matching the adjusted models in every section
adj_cov_formula <- ~ age + sex + ethn_binary + ukborn + urban + edu_qual + marstat + chron_health

# design-term values per section. each maps one grid row to the model's own term names, interactions included
its_design <- function(row) {
  t <- row$t; p <- row$post
  list(time_since_policy = t, post_policy_month = p,
       "time_since_policy:post_policy_month" = t * p)
}

pt_design <- function(row) {
  y <- row$pt_year; g <- row$family_3plus
  list(pt_year = y, family_3plus = g,
       "pt_year:family_3plus" = y * g)
}

did_design <- function(row) {
  g <- row$family_3plus; p <- row$did_post_period
  list(family_3plus = g, did_post_period = p,
       "family_3plus:did_post_period" = g * p)
}

cits_design <- function(row) {
  t <- row$t; p <- row$post; g <- row$family_3plus
  list(time_since_policy = t, post_policy_month = p, family_3plus = g,
       "time_since_policy:post_policy_month" = t * p,
       "time_since_policy:family_3plus" = t * g,
       "post_policy_month:family_3plus" = p * g,
       "time_since_policy:post_policy_month:family_3plus" = t * p * g)
}

# some strata contain a single primary sampling unit, and the survey package errors by default when a stratum has only one. "average" substitutes the average variance from the other strata, which is the option closest to Stata's singleunit(scaled) used in the Understanding Society guidance; "adjust" is the more conservative alternative
options(survey.lonely.psu = "average")

```

## Descriptives

The first step of analysis is obtaining descriptives. For all descriptives and analyses, these will be pooled values across all 20 imputed datasets. The first set of descriptives includes the 2017 data, as we are trying to obtain year-by-year estimates.

To start the descriptives section, I obtain a descriptive figure displaying the dose-response curve of the post-intervention treatment group.

For this, I am trying to obtain specific information on the proportion of affected individuals per year (after the policy was implemented) from the 3+ children group (because they are only considered "affected" if their third child was born after the two-child benefit cap was implemented) - noting that I am using interview year here as a proxy because we don't have information on month/day for birth.

```{r}
#| label: flow-table
#| code-summary: Sample flowchart counts
sample_flow

wb_flow <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb_flow, "Sample_Flow")
writeData(wb_flow, "Sample_Flow", sample_flow)
saveWorkbook(wb_flow, "output/Sample_Flow_20260812.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: figure-1-stacked-bar-graphs-showing-prop
#| code-summary: Stacked bar graph showing proportion of observations with 3+ kids affected by intervention vs those not every year from 2017
# creating stacked bar graph showing proportion of 3+ kids affected by intervention versus those who are not (so treated = NA vs treated = 1) every year from 2017 onwards - also using colour-blind friendly colours
# using interview year (not birth year) on the x-axis: the figure shows exposure accumulating in the sample over calendar time; birth year is already the classifier, since treated is defined by youngest_child_yob >= 2017
fig1_data <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(.imp > 0, family_3plus == 1, intyear >= 2017) %>%
  mutate(treatment_status = case_when(
    treated == 1 ~ "Affected (3rd+ child born 2017+)",
    is.na(treated) ~ "Unaffected (all children born pre-2017)",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) %>%
  mutate(treatment_status = factor(treatment_status, 
                                   levels = c("Unaffected (all children born pre-2017)",
                                              "Affected (3rd+ child born 2017+)"))) %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear, treatment_status) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(intyear, treatment_status) %>%
  summarise(pooled_prop = mean(prop), .groups = "drop")

pdf("output/treatment_proportion_20260812.pdf", width = 10, height = 6)
ggplot(fig1_data, aes(x = as.factor(intyear), y = pooled_prop, fill = treatment_status)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Unaffected (all children born pre-2017)" = "#56B4E9",
                               "Affected (3rd+ child born 2017+)" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(title = "Proportion Affected vs Unaffected over Years (3+ Children, 2017 onwards)",
       x = "Interview Year",
       y = "Proportion",
       fill = "Treatment Status") +
  theme_minimal()
dev.off()
```

Next, I move onto obtaining descriptive tables, which will be the majority of this section. The first set of descriptives I am obtaining will be Ns of each category (in this case, `treated` refers to being affected by the rollout of the two-child benefit cap, i.e. your 3rd child was born after the cutoff).

```{r}
#| label: table-1a-sample-sizes-ns-treated-family
#| code-summary: Family-level sample sizes table
# Ns treated (FAMILY-LEVEL counts)
family_level_table <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  group_by(.imp, hidp, intyear) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    group_1_2           = (family_3plus == 0),
    group_3plus         = (family_3plus == 1 & (intyear < 2017 | is.na(treated))),
    group_3plus_treated = (family_3plus == 1 & intyear >= 2017 & !is.na(treated) & treated == 1)
  ) %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    families_1_2           = sum(group_1_2, na.rm = TRUE),
    families_3plus         = sum(group_3plus, na.rm = TRUE),
    families_3plus_treated = sum(group_3plus_treated, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    f_1_2    = round(mean(families_1_2)),
    f_3plus  = round(mean(families_3plus)),
    f_treated = round(mean(families_3plus_treated)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Families 1-2 children`             = f_1_2,
    `Families 3+ children (unaffected)` = ifelse(f_3plus == 0, NA_real_, f_3plus),
    `Families 3+ children (affected)`   = ifelse(intyear < 2017, NA_real_, f_treated)
  ) %>%
  select(intyear, `Families 1-2 children`, `Families 3+ children (unaffected)`,
         `Families 3+ children (affected)`) %>%
  rename(Year = intyear)
```

```{r}
#| label: table-1a-sample-sizes-ns-treated-individ
#| code-summary: Observation-level sample sizes table
# Ns treated (OBSERVATION-LEVEL counts, i.e. person-years)
individual_level_table <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    group_1_2           = (family_3plus == 0),
    group_3plus         = (family_3plus == 1 & (intyear < 2017 | is.na(treated))),
    group_3plus_treated = (family_3plus == 1 & intyear >= 2017 & !is.na(treated) & treated == 1)
  ) %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    individuals_1_2           = sum(group_1_2, na.rm = TRUE),
    individuals_3plus         = sum(group_3plus, na.rm = TRUE),
    individuals_3plus_treated = sum(group_3plus_treated, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    i_1_2    = round(mean(individuals_1_2)),
    i_3plus  = round(mean(individuals_3plus)),
    i_treated = round(mean(individuals_3plus_treated)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Observations 1-2 children`             = i_1_2,
    `Observations 3+ children (unaffected)` = ifelse(i_3plus == 0, NA_real_, i_3plus),
    `Observations 3+ children (affected)`   = ifelse(intyear < 2017, NA_real_, i_treated)
  ) %>%
  select(intyear, `Observations 1-2 children`, `Observations 3+ children (unaffected)`,
         `Observations 3+ children (affected)`) %>%
  rename(Year = intyear)
```

Finally, we wanted to obtain means of all the outcomes by interview year and group, as well as the proportion of individuals in the treated group by year.

```{r}
#| label: table-2-means-90-cis-of-key-outcomes-by
#| code-summary: Means (90% CIs) of key outcomes by group and year
outcome_means_by_year_pooled <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  mutate(group = case_when(
    family_3plus == 0 ~ "1-2 children",
    family_3plus == 1 & post_policy_month == 0 ~ "3+ children",
    family_3plus == 1 & post_policy_month == 1 & intyear == 2017 & treated == 1  ~ "3+ children (treated)",
    family_3plus == 1 & post_policy_month == 1 & intyear == 2017 & is.na(treated) ~ "3+ children (unaffected)",
    family_3plus == 1 & post_policy_month == 1 & intyear >= 2018 & treated == 1  ~ "3+ children (treated)",
    family_3plus == 1 & post_policy_month == 1 & intyear >= 2018 & is.na(treated) ~ "3+ children (unaffected)",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c(
    "1-2 children", "3+ children",
    "3+ children (treated)", "3+ children (unaffected)"
  ))) %>%
  # pivot to long for cleaner pooling
  select(.imp, intyear, group, all_of(outcomes_raw)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(outcomes_raw), names_to = "outcome", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear, group, outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_val   = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_val    = sum(!is.na(value)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intyear, group, outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    pooled_mean = mean(mean_val),
    # Rubin's rules for the sampling variance of a mean:
    # within-imputation component is the mean of sd^2/n, NOT the mean of sd^2
    within_var  = mean(sd_val^2 / n_val),
    between_var = var(mean_val),
    pooled_se   = sqrt(within_var + (1 + 1/m_imp) * between_var),
    ci_lower    = pooled_mean - 1.645 * pooled_se,
    ci_upper    = pooled_mean + 1.645 * pooled_se,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    result  = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f - %.2f)", pooled_mean, ci_lower, ci_upper),
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = outcomes_raw, labels = outcome_labels)
  ) %>%
  select(intyear, group, outcome, result) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = result) %>%
  arrange(intyear, group) %>%
  rename(Year = intyear, Group = group)
```

```{r}
#| label: table-1a-supplement-proportion-of-treate
#| code-summary: Proportion of treated individuals within the 3+ children group by interview year
treated_proportions <- imp_long_full %>%
  filter(.imp > 0, family_3plus == 1, intyear >= 2018) %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total   = n(),
    n_treated = sum(treated == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intyear) %>%
  summarise(
    pooled_total   = round(mean(n_total)),
    pooled_treated = round(mean(n_treated)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pct_treated = round(pooled_treated / pooled_total * 100, 1)
  ) %>%
  rename(Year = intyear)
```

The subsequent tables generated below focus specifically on the analytic sample (excluding the individuals with their third or more child in 2017). These are total Ns for individuals and households by group (not by year, as done above).

```{r}
#| label: table-1b-overall-n-individuals-and-house
#| code-summary: Overall N individuals and households by group (analytic sample)
group_ns <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  mutate(group = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)")) %>%
  group_by(.imp, group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_individuals = n_distinct(pidp),
    n_households  = n_distinct(hidp),
    n_obs         = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    `N Individuals (unique)`  = round(mean(n_individuals)),
    `N Households (unique)`   = round(mean(n_households)),
    `N Observations (person-years)` = round(mean(n_obs)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The next steps will involve obtaining information on confounders - both the continuous and categorical ones, as well as the income quintiles - for the descriptives table.

```{r}
#| label: table-1c-sample-characteristics-control
#| code-summary: Means and SDs for covariates (analytic sample)

covariates_continuous  <- c("age", "equiv_yearly")
covariates_categorical <- c("sex", "ethn_binary", "ukborn", "urban", "edu_qual", "marstat", "oc_current", "chron_health")

# continuous covariates - pooled means and SDs
covariate_continuous_pooled <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  select(.imp, family_3plus, all_of(covariates_continuous)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(covariates_continuous), names_to = "covariate", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus, covariate) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_val   = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(family_3plus, covariate) %>%
  summarise(
    pooled_mean = mean(mean_val),
    pooled_sd   = sqrt(mean(sd_val^2)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    result = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", pooled_mean, pooled_sd),
    group  = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)")
  ) %>%
  select(covariate, group, result) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = result)

# categorical covariates - pooled proportions
# marstat and oc_current are factors; pivot_longer cannot combine factor and numeric columns, so everything is converted to character first
covariate_categorical_pooled <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  select(.imp, family_3plus, all_of(covariates_categorical)) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(covariates_categorical), as.character)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(covariates_categorical), names_to = "covariate", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus, covariate, value) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus, covariate) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(family_3plus, covariate, value) %>%
  summarise(
    pooled_prop = mean(prop),
    pooled_n    = mean(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    result          = sprintf("%.0f (%.1f%%)", pooled_n, pooled_prop * 100),
    group           = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)"),
    covariate_level = paste0(covariate, "_", value)
  ) %>%
  select(covariate_level, group, result) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = result)

# income quintiles - pooled proportions
# note: quintiles are computed in imp-recalc-quintiles on the full imputed data, so boundaries are fixed across all analytic subsets and counts here are not equal fifths
income_quintile_pooled <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  mutate(income_quintile_label = case_when(
    income_quintile == 1 ~ "Income quintile 1 (Lowest)",
    income_quintile == 2 ~ "Income quintile 2",
    income_quintile == 3 ~ "Income quintile 3",
    income_quintile == 4 ~ "Income quintile 4",
    income_quintile == 5 ~ "Income quintile 5 (Highest)",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )) %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus, income_quintile_label) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(family_3plus, income_quintile_label) %>%
  summarise(
    pooled_prop = mean(prop),
    pooled_n    = mean(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(income_quintile_label)) %>%
  mutate(
    result   = sprintf("%.0f (%.1f%%)", pooled_n, pooled_prop * 100),
    group    = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)"),
    variable = income_quintile_label
  ) %>%
  select(variable, group, result) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = result)

# combine continuous, categorical, and income quintiles
sample_characteristics_table <- bind_rows(
  covariate_continuous_pooled %>% rename(variable = covariate),
  covariate_categorical_pooled %>% rename(variable = covariate_level),
  income_quintile_pooled
)
```

This is additionally supplemented by information on descriptives for each outcome by group.

```{r}
#| label: table-1d-outcome-descriptives-by-group-p
#| code-summary: Outcome descriptives by group (means, SDs, range, N obs; analytic sample)
outcome_descriptives <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0) %>%
  mutate(group = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)")) %>%
```

## Correlation analyses

For this section, I will be generating correlation matrices for all of the outcomes, just to obtain some idea as to how related the outcomes might be (this is especially relevant for the HRQoL and self-rated health outcomes, as the self-rated health question is the first question of the HRQoL measure.)

Once again, this is pooled across 20 imputed datasets.

```{r}
#| label: pooled-correlation-matrix-across-imputat
#| code-summary: Correlation matrix
# pooled correlation matrix across imputations in analytic sample
# computed on raw outcomes - correlation is scale-invariant, so the z-scored versions give identical values
cor_matrices <- lapply(seq_len(m_imp), function(i) {
  imp_long_no2017 %>%
    filter(.imp == i) %>%
    select(all_of(outcomes_raw)) %>%
    cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
})

# pooling via Fisher z rather than averaging r directly - standard practice for imputations
z_matrices <- lapply(cor_matrices, atanh)
pooled_cor_matrix <- tanh(Reduce("+", z_matrices) / m_imp)
diag(pooled_cor_matrix) <- 1
colnames(pooled_cor_matrix) <- outcome_labels
rownames(pooled_cor_matrix) <- outcome_labels

# export numerical correlation matrix to excel
wb_cor <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb_cor, "Correlation_Matrix")
writeData(wb_cor, "Correlation_Matrix",
          as.data.frame(round(pooled_cor_matrix, 3)),
          rowNames = TRUE)
saveWorkbook(wb_cor, "output/Correlations_pooled_20260812.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

## Power analysis

For this section, I will be calculating minimum detectable effects (MDEs) for each outcome at the α = 0.1 level. This gives, based on the Ns used for each type of analysis below (which will be delineated), at 80% power, what the minimum effect is that we could detect, in raw point estimates and standardised units.

In order to account for clustering, we are calculating the design effect size (combination of ICC and average cluster size), then adjust power calculation by that magnitude for each outcome. Since we calculate one ICC, 

In addition to these calculations, these chunks calculate sample details, and then all results from the section are exported into an Excel workbook.

```{r}
#| label: power-design-constants
#| code-summary: Design constants for MDE calculations
# did_pre and did_post are defined in analysis-setup
z_sum <- qnorm(0.95) + qnorm(0.80)   # alpha = 0.10 two-sided, 80% power

# restricted to observations with a positive survey weight, since the analysis models are weighted and a zero-weighted observation contributes nothing to the estimates
d <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(.imp > 0, !is.na(time_since_policy), !is.na(post_policy_month), xs_weight > 0)

# cell sizes for the DiD level change, over the DiD window
n_cells <- d %>%
  filter(intyear %in% c(did_pre, did_post)) %>%
  mutate(post = as.integer(intyear %in% did_post)) %>%
  count(.imp, family_3plus, post) %>%
  group_by(family_3plus, post) %>%
  summarise(n = mean(n), .groups = "drop")

# spread of time within period for the ITS/CITS slope change, over the full series
ss_cells <- d %>%
  group_by(.imp, family_3plus, post_policy_month) %>%
  summarise(ss = (n() - 1) * var(time_since_policy), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(family_3plus, post_policy_month) %>%
  summarise(ss = mean(ss), .groups = "drop")

nn <- function(g, p) n_cells$n[n_cells$family_3plus == g & n_cells$post == p]
ss <- function(g, p) ss_cells$ss[ss_cells$family_3plus == g & ss_cells$post_policy_month == p]

se_its  <- sqrt(1/ss(1, 0) + 1/ss(1, 1))
se_did  <- sqrt(1/nn(1, 0) + 1/nn(1, 1) + 1/nn(0, 0) + 1/nn(0, 1))
se_cits <- sqrt(1/ss(1, 0) + 1/ss(1, 1) + 1/ss(0, 0) + 1/ss(0, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: power-icc
#| code-summary: Primary sampling unit ICC and design effect for the power calculations
# the MDE calculations above treat observations as independent, which they are not - observations cluster within primary sampling units, and clustering inflates the variance of an estimate without biasing it. the design effect quantifies that inflation as DEFF = 1 + (m - 1) * ICC, where m is the average cluster size and ICC is the share of total outcome variance sitting between primary sampling units rather than within them. standard errors, and therefore minimum detectable effects, inflate by sqrt(DEFF)
# the primary sampling unit is used rather than the household because that is the level the analysis models cluster on, so the design effect describes the same variance structure as the reported standard errors
# ICC is estimated by one-way ANOVA on the primary sampling unit, using the unbalanced-design correction for average cluster size, computed within each imputation and averaged across them. it is scale-invariant, so raw and z-scored outcomes give identical values
compute_icc <- function(outcome_var, data) {
  per_imp <- data %>%
    filter(.imp > 0, !is.na(.data[[outcome_var]])) %>%
    group_by(.imp) %>%
    group_modify(function(d, ...) {
      cl <- d %>%
        group_by(psu) %>%
        summarise(n_i = n(), mean_i = mean(.data[[outcome_var]]), .groups = "drop")
      N <- sum(cl$n_i)
      a <- nrow(cl)
      grand <- sum(cl$n_i * cl$mean_i) / N
      msb <- sum(cl$n_i * (cl$mean_i - grand)^2) / (a - 1)
      msw <- sum((d[[outcome_var]] - cl$mean_i[match(d$psu, cl$psu)])^2) / (N - a)
      # k0 is the average cluster size corrected for unequal cluster sizes
      k0 <- (N - sum(cl$n_i^2) / N) / (a - 1)
      tibble(icc = max(0, (msb - msw) / (msb + (k0 - 1) * msw)))
    })
  mean(per_imp$icc)
}

icc_by_outcome <- data.frame(
  Outcome = outcome_labels,
  ICC     = vapply(outcomes_raw, function(v) compute_icc(v, d), numeric(1))
)
icc_by_outcome

# a single ICC is used for the power calculations rather than one per outcome, so that a single design effect can be reported
icc_mean <- mean(icc_by_outcome$ICC)

# average cluster size within each analysis sample, since the three methods estimate on different samples
mbar <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    filter(.imp > 0) %>%
    count(.imp, psu) %>%
    group_by(.imp) %>%
    summarise(m = mean(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pull(m) %>%
    mean()
}

mbar_its  <- mbar(d %>% filter(family_3plus == 1))
mbar_did  <- mbar(d %>% filter(intyear %in% c(did_pre, did_post)))
mbar_cits <- mbar(d)

deff_its  <- 1 + (mbar_its  - 1) * icc_mean
deff_did  <- 1 + (mbar_did  - 1) * icc_mean
deff_cits <- 1 + (mbar_cits - 1) * icc_mean

design_effects <- data.frame(
  Analysis          = c("ITS", "DiD", "CITS"),
  Mean_cluster_size = c(mbar_its, mbar_did, mbar_cits),
  ICC               = icc_mean,
  DEFF              = c(deff_its, deff_did, deff_cits),
  SE_inflation      = sqrt(c(deff_its, deff_did, deff_cits))
)
design_effects
```

```{r}
#| label: compute-pooled-stats-n-mean-sd-by-treatm
#| code-summary: Computing pooled stats by treatment group for power analyses
# compute pooled stats (n, mean, sd) by treatment group for power analyses
compute_power_stats <- function(outcome_var, data) {
  data %>%
    filter(.imp > 0) %>%
    group_by(.imp, family_3plus) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_val = mean(.data[[outcome_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_val = sd(.data[[outcome_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    group_by(family_3plus) %>%
    summarise(
      pooled_n = mean(n),
      pooled_mean = mean(mean_val),
      # pooled SD of the variable = mean of the within-imputation variances
      pooled_sd = sqrt(mean(sd_val^2)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

power_results <- map_dfr(seq_along(outcomes_raw), function(j) {
  pd <- compute_power_stats(outcomes_raw[j], d)
  p_sd <- sqrt(sum((pd$pooled_n - 1) * pd$pooled_sd^2) / sum(pd$pooled_n - 1))
  se   <- c(se_its, se_did, se_cits)
  # the design effect uses this outcome's own ICC, since the share of variance sitting between primary sampling units differs by outcome, combined with the average cluster size for each method's analysis sample
  icc_j <- icc_by_outcome$ICC[j]
  deff <- 1 + (c(mbar_its, mbar_did, mbar_cits) - 1) * icc_j

  n_trt_full  <- pd$pooled_n[pd$family_3plus == 1]
  n_ctrl_full <- pd$pooled_n[pd$family_3plus == 0]

  data.frame(
    Outcome      = outcome_labels[j],
    Analysis     = c("ITS", "DiD", "CITS"),
    Estimand     = c("Slope change (per year)", "Level change", "Differential slope change (per year)"),
    Alpha        = 0.10,
    Power        = 0.80,
    # ITS and CITS use the full series; DiD uses the pre/post windows only
    N_Treatment  = c(n_trt_full, nn(1, 0) + nn(1, 1), n_trt_full),
    N_Control    = c(NA,         nn(0, 0) + nn(0, 1), n_ctrl_full),
    Pooled_SD    = p_sd,
    ICC          = icc_j,
    # unadjusted values treat observations as independent
    MDE_SD_units = z_sum * se,
    MDE_Raw      = z_sum * se * p_sd,
    # adjusted values inflate by sqrt(DEFF) to account for clustering within primary sampling units
    DEFF                  = deff,
    MDE_SD_units_adjusted = z_sum * se * sqrt(deff),
    MDE_Raw_adjusted      = z_sum * se * sqrt(deff) * p_sd
  )
})
```

```{r}
#| label: sample-details-for-all-outcomes
#| code-summary: Sample details for all outcomes
sample_details <- map_dfr(seq_along(outcomes_raw), function(j) {
  pd <- compute_power_stats(outcomes_raw[j], imp_long_no2017)
  pd %>%
    mutate(
      Outcome = outcome_labels[j],
      Group = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)")
    ) %>%
    select(Outcome, Group, N = pooled_n, Mean = pooled_mean, SD = pooled_sd)
})
```

```{r}

#| code-summary: Exporting power analysis results
wb_power <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb_power, "Power_Analysis")
writeData(wb_power, "Power_Analysis", power_results)
addWorksheet(wb_power, "Sample_Details")
writeData(wb_power, "Sample_Details", sample_details)
addWorksheet(wb_power, "ICC_Design_Effects")
writeData(wb_power, "ICC_Design_Effects", icc_by_outcome)
writeData(wb_power, "ICC_Design_Effects", design_effects, startRow = nrow(icc_by_outcome) + 3)
saveWorkbook(wb_power, "output/Power_Analysis_20260817.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

## Interrupted time series (ITS) analyses

For interrupted time series analyses, I'm running unadjusted, adjusted, and standardised (z-score) adjusted models for each outcome. These models will be pooled over the 20 datasets and run for the full model, as well as subgroup analyses for sex (male/female), ethnicity (white/ethnic minority), and income quintile (bottom 2/top 3).

### Full models

#### Unadjusted (raw)

```{r}
#| label: its-ghq-total
#| code-summary: Psychological distress
its_GHQ_full_unadj <- lapply(1:imp_its$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_its, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
  svyglm(GHQ_total ~ time_since_policy + post_policy_month + time_since_policy:post_policy_month,
         design = design_i)
})
class(its_GHQ_full_unadj) <- c("mira", "list")
its_GHQ_full_unadj_pooled <- mice::pool(its_GHQ_full_unadj)
summary(its_GHQ_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90)
```

```{r}
#| label: its-life-sat
#| code-summary: Life satisfaction
its_life_sat_full_unadj <- lapply(1:imp_its$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_its, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
```

#### Adjusted (raw)

As a refresher, this includes the following confounders after imputation:

- age (`age`)

- sex (`sex`)

- ethnicity (`ethn_binary`)

- country of birth (`ukborn`)

- urbanicity (`urban`)

- highest education level (`edu_qual`)

- de facto marital status (`marstat`)

- chronic health condition (`chron_health`)

We no longer include household income (`equiv_yearly`) or current occupation class (`oc_current`) in analyses due them could arguably being on the causal pathway, and therefore should not be controlled for.

```{r}
#| label: ghq-total-2
#| code-summary: Psychological distress
its_GHQ_full_adj <- lapply(1:imp_its$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_its, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
  svyglm(GHQ_total ~ time_since_policy + post_policy_month + time_since_policy:post_policy_month + age + sex + ethn_binary + ukborn + urban + edu_qual + marstat + chron_health,
         design = design_i)
})

pooled_its_GHQ_full_adj <- mice::pool(its_GHQ_full_adj)
```

### Subgroup analyses

For all subgroup analyses, I am running them on standardised adjusted models for two reasons: 1) these are the most comprehensive models, and 2) for simplicity's sake, as running subgroup analyses on all the models run above would mean there are hundreds more models that are anyway less specific.

#### Sex subgroups

##### Male

```{r}
#| label: ghq-total-z-male
#| code-summary: Psychological distress
its_GHQ_male_adj_z <- lapply(1:imp_its$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_its, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
  # the design is subset rather than the data, so that the full stratum and cluster structure is retained for variance estimation
  svyglm(GHQ_total_z ~ time_since_policy + post_policy_month + time_since_policy:post_policy_month + age + ethn_binary + ukborn + urban + edu_qual + marstat + chron_health,
         design = subset(design_i, sex == 1))
})
class(its_GHQ_male_adj_z) <- c("mira", "list")
pooled_its_GHQ_male_adj_z <- mice::pool(its_GHQ_male_adj_z)
```

### Data exporting

#### Generating tables

Then, the following chunk of code creates an ITS results workbook, containing the following:

- unadjusted raw results

- adjusted raw results

- standardised adjusted results

- subgroup analyses (sex)

- subgroup analyses (ethnicity)

- subgroup analyses (income quintiles)

- a formatted summary table of 1-3, including coefficients and 90% CIs for the full analyses

- a formatted summary table of 4-6 for each group, including coefficients and 90% CIs for each subgroup

The last two bullet points here will be what goes into the tables for the manuscript/supplement.

```{r}
#| label: its-excel-export
#| code-summary: Generating ITS Excel workbook
## ITS Excel export
# create workbook for ITS results
wb_its <- createWorkbook()

# unadjusted (raw)
addWorksheet(wb_its, "ITS_Full_Unadj")
its_tab_unadj <- bind_rows(
  summary(its_GHQ_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),
  summary(its_life_sat_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction"),
  summary(its_self_health_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health"),
  summary(its_SF_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL"),
  summary(its_health_sat_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction"),
  summary(its_finnow_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation"),
  summary(its_finfut_full_unadj_pooled, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook")
) %>%
  filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "time_since_policy", "post_policy_month",
                     "time_since_policy:post_policy_month"))
writeData(wb_its, "ITS_Full_Unadj", its_tab_unadj)

# adjusted (raw)

  summary(pooled_its_GHQ_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),

) %>%
```

#### Generating figures

First, I run some helper functions that will help with running the tasks. These do the following:

For generating figures with predicted marginal means for all seven outcomes:

- building pooled observed means for an outcome

- computing predicted marginal means from the fitted models, averaged over the observed covariate distribution within each imputation and then across imputations

- making the ITS panels with predicted marginal means

```{r}
#| label: its-figure-helpers
#| code-summary: ITS figure helpers
# helper: build pooled observed means for one outcome (3+ families only)
build_its_plot_data <- function(outcome_var, data_long) {
  data_long %>%
    filter(.imp > 0, family_3plus == 1) %>%
    group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%
    summarise(mean_val = mean(.data[[outcome_var]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(intyear) %>%
    summarise(pooled_mean = mean(mean_val), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(intyear != 2017) %>%
    mutate(post = as.integer(intyear > 2017))
}

# covariate means for the ITS marginal means, computed once
its_xbar <- covariate_means(imp_long_its, adj_cov_formula)

# helper: the three fitted lines for one outcome, with 90% CIs. counterfactual = post-policy years evaluated with post_policy_month = 0
# the fitted lines are evaluated at (year - 2017), matching the CITS figures. evaluating instead at the mean observed interview timing within each year makes consecutive years unevenly spaced in time while the axis spaces them evenly, so a line that is straight in the model appears to curve
build_its_lines <- function(model_list, plot_data) {
  yr_min <- min(plot_data$intyear)
  yr_max <- max(plot_data$intyear)
  pre_years  <- seq(yr_min, 2016)
  post_years <- seq(2018, yr_max)
  tv <- function(yrs) yrs - 2017

  mm <- function(yrs, post_value) {
    grid <- data.frame(year = yrs, t = tv(yrs), post = post_value)
    marginal_means_fits(model_list, its_xbar, grid, its_design) %>%
      select(year, y = pooled_mean, ci_lower, ci_upper)
  }

  list(
    pre         = mm(pre_years,  0),
    post        = mm(post_years, 1),
    counterfact = mm(post_years, 0)
  )
}

# helper: one ITS panel. shared_ylim = NULL leaves the panel free-scaled; zero_line adds a dotted reference at 0 for the standardised version
make_its_panel <- function(plot_data, lines, outcome_label, outcome_ylab,
                           shared_ylim = NULL, zero_line = FALSE) {
  yr_min <- min(plot_data$intyear)
  yr_max <- max(plot_data$intyear)

  p <- ggplot()
  if (zero_line) {
    p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40",
                        linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted")
  }
  p <- p +
    # 90% CI bands, drawn first and lighter than the observed points so the points stay legible on top. no band on the counterfactual, which is a hypothetical rather than an estimate of anything observed
    geom_ribbon(data = lines$pre, aes(x = year, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
                fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15) +
    geom_ribbon(data = lines$post, aes(x = year, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
                fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15) +
    # observed means as transparent dots
    geom_point(data = plot_data, aes(x = intyear, y = pooled_mean),
               colour = "#0072B2", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    # pre-policy fitted line
    geom_line(data = lines$pre, aes(x = year, y = y),
              colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.1) +
    # post-policy actual fitted line
    geom_line(data = lines$post, aes(x = year, y = y),
              colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.1) +
    # counterfactual
    geom_line(data = lines$counterfact, aes(x = year, y = y),
              colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "22") +
    # policy line
    geom_vline(xintercept = 2017, colour = "#D55E00",
               linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(yr_min, yr_max, by = 2)) +
    labs(title = outcome_label, x = "", y = outcome_ylab) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
          axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

  if (!is.null(shared_ylim)) p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = shared_ylim)
  p
}

# create a dummy plot for the ITS legend, built once and reused by both figures. the confidence band is represented by a wide semi-transparent line segment, since a ribbon cannot be drawn into a legend key directly
its_legend_source <- ggplot() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1.5, colour = "Two-child benefit cap\nintroduction (2017)"), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1, y = 1, colour = "Observed mean"), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(x = c(1, 2), y = c(1, 2), colour = "Fitted trend"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(x = c(1, 2), y = c(1, 2), colour = "90% confidence band"), linewidth = 6, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(aes(x = c(1, 2), y = c(1, 1.5), colour = "Counterfactual"), linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "22") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "",
    values = c("Two-child benefit cap\nintroduction (2017)" = "#D55E00",
               "Observed mean" = "#0072B2", "Fitted trend" = "#0072B2",
               "90% confidence band" = "#0072B2", "Counterfactual" = "#0072B2"),
    breaks = c("Two-child benefit cap\nintroduction (2017)", "Observed mean",
               "Fitted trend", "90% confidence band", "Counterfactual"),
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      shape     = c(NA, 16, NA, NA, NA),
      linetype  = c("dashed", "blank", "solid", "solid", "22"),
      linewidth = c(0.8, NA, 1.1, 6, 0.7),
      alpha     = c(1, 0.3, 1, 0.15, 1)
    ))
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "center", legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

its_legend_panel <- make_legend_panel(its_legend_source)
```

```{r}
    subtitle = "Marginal means shown, with 90% confidence bands. Higher scores indicate worse outcomes.",

    )
  )

pdf("output/ITS_all_outcomes_multipanel_20260817.pdf", width = 16, height = 9)
print(its_combined)
dev.off()
```

```{r}
# shared symmetric y-axis range, computed from the confidence bands as well as the observed means so that coord_cartesian cannot clip a band or a line at the panel edge
its_z_all_vals <- c(
  unlist(map(its_plot_data_all_z, ~ .x$pooled_mean)),
  unlist(map(its_lines_all_z, ~ c(.x$pre$ci_lower, .x$pre$ci_upper,
                                  .x$post$ci_lower, .x$post$ci_upper,
                                  .x$counterfact$y)))
)
its_z_ylim <- c(min(its_z_all_vals, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.15,
                max(its_z_all_vals, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.15)
its_z_ylim <- c(-max(abs(its_z_ylim)), max(abs(its_z_ylim)))

its_panels_z <- pmap(list(seq_along(outcomes_raw), outcome_labels, outcome_ylabs),
                     function(j, label, ylab) {

                 shared_ylim = its_z_ylim, zero_line = TRUE)
})

  (its_panels_z[[5]] | its_panels_z[[6]] | its_panels_z[[7]] | its_legend_panel) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Changes in parental outcomes over time following the two-child benefit cap implementation",
    subtitle = "Marginal means on standardised scale from interrupted time series models shown, with 90% confidence bands. Higher scores indicate worse outcomes.",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
    )
  )

pdf("output/ITS_all_outcomes_multipanel_zscore_20260817.pdf", width = 16, height = 9)
print(its_combined_z)
dev.off()
```

## Difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses

We are structuring our DiD to focus on using 2014 to 2016 as the "before" timepoint and 2023 onwards as the "after" time point, as by then, all 3+ children families included in the study would have been affected by the policy.

However, before any DiD (or CITS, later on) are run, the parallel trends assumption needs to be tested.

### Parallel trends assumption testing

In essence, what this means is that we need to check whether both 3+ children (affected) and 1-2 children (control) groups were moving in the same direction between two time points before the implementation, otherwise it can be hard to parse out whether the change seen (if any) after the implementation in the affected group is because of the policy.

#### Numerical parallel trends testing

For the numerical tests, the parallel trends assumption is testing the interaction between `pt_year`  and `family_3plus` (the binary indicator of whether an individual has either 3+ children or 1-2 children). If the interaction is significant, the parallel trends assumption is violated. I test this for unadjusted (raw), adjusted (raw), and standardised adjusted models for each outcome, before then generating an Excel workbook with all the results (same workflow for ITS, which I adapt for all subsequent numerical models too).

##### Unadjusted (raw) parallel trends

```{r}
#| label: ghq-total-3
#| code-summary: Psychological distress
parallel_trends_GHQ <- lapply(1:imp_pt$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_pt, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
  svyglm(GHQ_total ~ pt_year * family_3plus,
         design = design_i)
})
class(parallel_trends_GHQ) <- c("mira", "list")
pooled_parallel_GHQ <- mice::pool(parallel_trends_GHQ)
summary(pooled_parallel_GHQ, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90)
```

#### Data exporting

##### Generating tables

```{r}
#| label: pt-excel-export
#| code-summary: Generating PT Excel workbook
## Parallel trends Excel export
wb_parallel <- createWorkbook()

# unadjusted (raw)
addWorksheet(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Unadj")
pt_tab_unadj <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_parallel_GHQ, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_life_sat, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_self_health, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_SF, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_health_sat, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finnow, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finfut, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook")
) %>%
filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "pt_year", "family_3plus",
                             "pt_year:family_3plus"))
writeData(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Unadj", pt_tab_unadj)

# adjusted (raw)
addWorksheet(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Adj")
pt_tab_adj <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_parallel_GHQ_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_life_sat_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_self_health_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_SF_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_health_sat_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finnow_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finfut_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook")
) %>%
filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "pt_year", "family_3plus",
                             "pt_year:family_3plus"))
writeData(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Adj", pt_tab_adj)

# standardised adjusted
addWorksheet(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Adj_Z")
pt_tab_adj_z <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_parallel_GHQ_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_life_sat_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_self_health_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_SF_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_health_sat_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finnow_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_parallel_finfut_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook (standardised)")
) %>%
filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "pt_year", "family_3plus",
                             "pt_year:family_3plus"))
writeData(wb_parallel, "PT_Full_Adj_Z", pt_tab_adj_z)

# subgroup analyses - sex
addWorksheet(wb_parallel, "PT_Subgroup_Sex")
```

#### Visual parallel trends testing

Even though we'll test it numerically, it makes sense to have a visual representation of this as well, as it'll be helpful to once again compare across outcomes and we'll have a better idea of what these numbers mean.

For this, I'll specifically be comparing the time periods 2009-2013 and 2014-2016 and generating a parallel trends figure using the standardised adjusted scoring (shared y-axis, 0 midpoint).

With this figure, as well as with all the other figures generated onwards, I'll be using the same workflow/setup as the ITS-generated figures in terms of pooling results and generating a multipanel figure including each outcome, with the 8th panel being the legend.

Visually, if the lines are regressing towards the mean, then that may be an indication that the parallel trends assumption could be violated.

##### Figure generation

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-helpers
#| code-summary: Parallel trends figure helpers
# helper: build pooled observed means by year for one outcome, both groups
build_pt_plot_data <- function(outcome_var, data_long) {
  data_long %>%
    filter(.imp > 0) %>%
    group_by(.imp, intyear, family_3plus) %>%
    summarise(mean_val = mean(.data[[outcome_var]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(intyear, family_3plus) %>%
    summarise(pooled_mean = mean(mean_val), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(group = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)"))
}

# covariate means for the PT marginal means, computed once
pt_xbar <- covariate_means(imp_long_pt, adj_cov_formula)

# the fitted lines are evaluated at every pre-policy year for each group
pt_grid <- expand.grid(pt_year = pt_years - max(pt_years), family_3plus = c(0, 1)) %>%
  mutate(intyear = pt_year + max(pt_years))

# helper: the two fitted trends for one outcome, with 90% CIs
build_pt_lines <- function(model_list) {
  marginal_means_fits(model_list, pt_xbar, pt_grid, pt_design) %>%
    mutate(group = ifelse(family_3plus == 0, "Control (1-2 children)", "Treatment (3+ children)"))
}

# helper: one PT panel
make_pt_panel <- function(plot_data, lines, outcome_label, outcome_ylab, shared_ylim) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted") +
    # 90% CI band around each fitted trend, lighter than the observed points so the points stay legible on top
    geom_ribbon(data = lines,
                aes(x = intyear, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper, fill = group),
                alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
    # observed yearly means as transparent dots
    geom_point(data = plot_data,
               aes(x = intyear, y = pooled_mean, colour = group, shape = group),
               size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    # fitted trends
    geom_line(data = lines,
              aes(x = intyear, y = pooled_mean, colour = group),
              linewidth = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(
      "Control (1-2 children)"  = "#E69F00",
      "Treatment (3+ children)" = "#0072B2"
    ), labels = c(
      "Control (1-2 children)"  = "1-2 children (control)",
      "Treatment (3+ children)" = "3+ children"
    )) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(
      "Control (1-2 children)"  = "#E69F00",
      "Treatment (3+ children)" = "#0072B2"
    ), guide = "none") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(
      "Control (1-2 children)"  = 16,
      "Treatment (3+ children)" = 15
    ), labels = c(
      "Control (1-2 children)"  = "1-2 children (control)",
      "Treatment (3+ children)" = "3+ children"
    )) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(pt_years), max(pt_years), by = 2)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = shared_ylim) +
    labs(title = outcome_label, x = "", y = outcome_ylab,
         colour = "Group", shape = "Group") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
      legend.position  = "none",
      axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-data
#| code-summary: Parallel trends figure data — observed means and fitted trends
# un-pooled model lists, in outcomes_raw order. the PT figure uses the standardised adjusted models, matching the corresponding table column
pt_adj_z_model_lists <- list(
  parallel_trends_GHQ_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_life_sat_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_self_health_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_SF_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_health_sat_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_finnow_adj_z,
  parallel_trends_finfut_adj_z
)

pt_plot_data_all <- map(outcomes_z_names, ~build_pt_plot_data(.x, imp_long_pt))
pt_lines_all <- map(seq_along(outcomes_z_names), function(j) {
  build_pt_lines(pt_adj_z_model_lists[[j]])
})
```

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-ylim
#| code-summary: Shared symmetric y-axis range for PT panels
# uses the CI bounds of the fitted trends as well as the observed means, so neither a band nor a point is clipped
pt_z_all_vals <- c(unlist(map(pt_plot_data_all, ~ .x$pooled_mean)),
                   unlist(map(pt_lines_all, ~ c(.x$ci_lower, .x$ci_upper))))
pt_z_ylim <- c(min(pt_z_all_vals, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.05,
               max(pt_z_all_vals, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.05)
pt_z_ylim <- c(-max(abs(pt_z_ylim)), max(abs(pt_z_ylim)))
```

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-panels
#| code-summary: Parallel trends panels, all 7 outcomes
pt_panels_z <- pmap(list(seq_along(outcomes_z_names), outcome_labels, outcome_ylabs),
                    function(j, label, ylab) {
  make_pt_panel(pt_plot_data_all[[j]], pt_lines_all[[j]], label, ylab, pt_z_ylim)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-legend
#| code-summary: Parallel trends legend panel
pt_legend_source <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1, y = 1, colour = "3+ children"), size = 3, shape = 15) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1, y = 1, colour = "1-2 children (control)"), size = 3, shape = 16) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "",
    values = c("3+ children" = "#0072B2",
               "1-2 children (control)" = "#E69F00"),
    breaks = c("3+ children", "1-2 children (control)"),
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      shape = c(15, 16)
    ))
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "center", legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

pt_legend_z <- make_legend_panel(pt_legend_source)
```

##### Exporting results

```{r}
#| label: pt-figure-export
#| code-summary: Assembling and exporting the parallel trends multipanel figure
pt_combined_z <- (pt_panels_z[[1]] | pt_panels_z[[2]] | pt_panels_z[[3]] | pt_panels_z[[4]]) /
  (pt_panels_z[[5]] | pt_panels_z[[6]] | pt_panels_z[[7]] | pt_legend_z) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Parallel Trends Test: All Outcomes (standardised)",
    subtitle = "Marginal means on standardised scale shown, with 90% confidence bands. Observed yearly means shown as points. Pre-policy years only (2009-2016). Higher scores indicate worse outcomes.",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8)
    )
  )

pdf("output/parallel_trends_all_outcomes_multipanel_zscore_20260817.pdf", width = 16, height = 9)
print(pt_combined_z)
dev.off()
```

### Classic DiD analysis: 2014-2016 vs 2023-2025

Our main difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses focuses on comparing the pre-benefit cap sample to only years where every third or more child born would have been affected by the two child benefit cap (2023 onwards, as demonstrated by the dose-response figure).

As there are three years of data present in the "post" timepoint (2023, 2024, and 2025), we use the three most recent years preceding the implementation of the two-child benefit cap (2014, 2015, and 2016) as the "pre" timepoint.

(We additionally run a DiD analysis using propensity score matching on the entire post-intervention sample, but this is done in the sensitivity analyses section below).

For DiD analyses, I'm following the same structure as ITS: I'm running unadjusted, adjusted, and standardised (z-score) adjusted models for each outcome. These models will be pooled over the 20 datasets and run for the full model, as well as subgroup analyses for sex (male/female), ethnicity (white/ethnic minority), and income quintile (bottom 2/top 3).

```{r}
#| label: did-setup
#| code-summary: Filtering to the relevant DiD time windows
# windows read from analysis-setup rather than hardcoded
imp_long_classic <- imp_long_no2017 %>%
  filter(intyear %in% c(did_pre, did_post)) %>%
  mutate(did_post_period = as.integer(intyear %in% did_post))   # 0 = 2014-2016, 1 = 2023-2025
imp_classic <- as.mids(imp_long_classic)
```

#### Full models

```{r}
#| label: ghq-total-did
#| code-summary: Psychological distress
did_GHQ_full_unadj <- lapply(1:imp_classic$m, function(i) {
  data_i <- mice::complete(imp_classic, i)
  design_i <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~xs_weight, data = data_i, nest = TRUE)
  svyglm(GHQ_total ~ family_3plus * did_post_period,
         design = design_i)
})
class(did_GHQ_full_unadj) <- c("mira", "list")
pooled_did_GHQ_full_unadj <- mice::pool(did_GHQ_full_unadj)
summary(pooled_did_GHQ_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90)
```

#### Data exporting

##### Generating tables

For this, I follow the same structure as ITS above.

```{r}
#| label: did-excel-export
#| code-summary: Generating classic DiD Excel workbook
## Classic DiD Excel export
# create workbook for Classic DiD results
wb_did <- createWorkbook()

# unadjusted (raw)
addWorksheet(wb_did, "DiD_Full_Unadj")
did_tab_unadj <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_did_GHQ_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),
  summary(pooled_did_life_sat_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_did_self_health_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health"),
  summary(pooled_did_SF_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL"),
  summary(pooled_did_health_sat_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_did_finnow_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation"),
  summary(pooled_did_finfut_full_unadj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook")
) %>%
  filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "family_3plus", "did_post_period",
                     "family_3plus:did_post_period"))
writeData(wb_did, "DiD_Full_Unadj", did_tab_unadj)

# adjusted (raw)
addWorksheet(wb_did, "DiD_Full_Adj")
did_tab_adj <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_did_GHQ_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress"),
  summary(pooled_did_life_sat_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_did_self_health_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health"),
  summary(pooled_did_SF_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL"),
  summary(pooled_did_health_sat_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Health satisfaction"),
  summary(pooled_did_finnow_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial situation"),
  summary(pooled_did_finfut_full_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Financial outlook")
) %>%
  filter(term %in% c("(Intercept)", "family_3plus", "did_post_period",
                     "family_3plus:did_post_period"))
writeData(wb_did, "DiD_Full_Adj", did_tab_adj)

# standardised adjusted
addWorksheet(wb_did, "DiD_Full_Adj_Z")
did_tab_adj_z <- bind_rows(
  summary(pooled_did_GHQ_full_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Psychological distress (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_did_life_sat_full_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Life satisfaction (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_did_self_health_full_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "Self-rated health (standardised)"),
  summary(pooled_did_SF_full_adj_z, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90) %>% mutate(outcome = "HRQoL (standardised)"),
```
